  46 Abstract


 47 Objective To estimate the incidence and recurrence rate of acute hamstring injuries in all levels of

 48 soccer.


 49 Study design Epidemiology systematic review


 50 Literature search We searched the PubMed (including Medline), CINAHL, SPORTDiscus, Embase

 51 and CENTRAL electronic databases.


 52 Study selection criteria We included prospective studies of all levels of adult soccer players that




Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
 53 registered acute hamstring injuries and provided a description of incidence of acute hamstring injuries

 54 in n/1000 playing hours (or available data to calculate this).


 55 Data synthesis Due to heterogeneity, we synthesised the data descriptively.


 56 Results Thirteen studies including 3868 players met the inclusion criteria. Two of thirteen included

 57 studies reported on hamstring injuries in women and thirteen on men. The incidence of acute




Downloaded from www.jospt.org at Ohio State University on December 15, 2020. For personal use only. No other uses without permission.
 58 hamstring injury ranged from 0.3 to 0.5 per 1000 exposure hours in women and 0.3 to 1.9 per 1000

 59 exposure hours in men. Hamstring injuries accounted for 5% to 15% of all soccer-related injuries.

 60 Hamstring injury recurrence rates ranged from 4% to 68%, depending on the injury definition.

 61 Certainty of the evidence ranged from moderate to very low.


 62 Conclusion The incidence of acute hamstring injury in soccer was 0.3 to 1.9 per 1000 exposure hours.




Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
 63 The recurrence rate was 4-68%. Certainty of the evidence ranged from moderate to very low.


 64 Key Words: Epidemiology/survey research, Lower extremity, Prevention (injury),
 65 Soccer, Systematic review/meta-analysis




 3
  66 Introduction


 67 Soccer (football) has over 265 million active players worldwide.11 Healthy lifestyle, positive influence

 68 on development and education of children and economic advantages are just some of the benefits from

 69 participation in soccer.7,8,13,24 Despite its positive effects, the risk of injuries in matches (i.e. game) and

 70 practice (training) is relatively high. Soccer accounts for the largest number of hospital-treated sports

 71 injuries in the European Union (>1.5 million visits).2


 72 An acute hamstring injury is frequently reported as one of the most common soccer injuries,3,10 but the




Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
 73 incidence of acute hamstring injuries in soccer is unclear. Accurate information about the incidence of

 74 acute hamstring injuries helps quantify the injury burden, and guides resource allocation for hamstring

 75 injury prevention. Understanding injury incidence may also help team doctors and physical therapists

 76 to make better decisions in targeting strategies for the prevention and rehabilitation of soccer injuries.


 77 The purpose of this systematic review was to estimate the incidence and recurrence rate of acute

 78 hamstring injuries in soccer.

 4
  79 Methods


 80 This review was prospectively registered in PROSPERO, the International Prospective Register of

 81 Systematic Reviews (CRD42016039011). The Preferred Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-

 82 Analysis (PRISMA) statement were followed in preparing, conducting and reporting this systematic

 83 review.25


 84


 85 Research question and outcomes




Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
 86 Our primary research aim was to estimate the incidence of acute hamstring (posterior thigh) injuries

 87 (indirect structural muscle injury26) during training and matches in adult male and female soccer of all

 88 playing levels.


 89 The primary outcomes were: 1) incidence rate in n/1000 playing hours during training and match play,

 90 2) incidence proportion, i.e. the proportion of hamstring injuries out of the total injuries in soccer.




Downloaded from www.jospt.org at Ohio State University on December 15, 2020. For personal use only. No other uses without permission.
 91 Our secondary aim was to estimate the recurrence rate of acute hamstring injuries12 during training and

 92 match play in adult male and female soccer of all playing levels as a proportion of the total injuries in

 93 soccer.


 94 Acute hamstring injuries were defined as any suddenly occurring, indirect, structural muscle injury to

 95 the hamstrings or the posterior thigh, sustained during soccer match or training, causing tissue injury,




Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
 96 time loss or the need for medical assistance.

 97

 98 Inclusion criteria for studies


 99 Studies were required to meet the following criteria: (1) prospective design, (2) adult soccer players

 100 (age ≥18 years), (3) soccer-specific population (11-a-side), all levels of competition, (4) full text report

 101 available, (5) description of at least one primary outcome, (6) acute hamstring injuries, defined as

 102 acute onset, acute injuries to the posterior thigh, presentation within 7 days of injury, and (7)



 5
  103 hamstring injury causing either: tissue injury12,17, time loss12, or the need for medical assistance12. We

 104 used previously defined, well-accepted definitions of acute hamstring injury.12,17 (Box 1)


 105


 106 Literature search


 107 A sensitive search strategy was constructed and executed with the assistance of a research librarian.

 108 The search strategy consisted of indexed and free text terms. Examples of search terms used were:

 109 ‘hamstring’, ‘thigh’, ‘semitendinosus’, ‘semimembranosus’, ‘biceps femoris’, ‘injury’, ‘rupture’,




Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
 110 ‘sprain’, ‘strain’, ‘tear’, ‘epidemiology’, ‘incidence’, ‘occurrence’, ‘soccer’, ‘football’ (full search

 111 available in supplementary appendix 1). Electronic databases (PubMed (including MEDLINE),

 112 CINAHL, SPORTDiscus, Embase and Cochrane) were searched by one investigator (WD) for eligible

 113 studies without language or time restriction, from their inception until August 6th 2019. All references

 114 of the primarily selected articles and recent systematic reviews were searched manually for potentially

 115 relevant articles.




Downloaded from www.jospt.org at Ohio State University on December 15, 2020. For personal use only. No other uses without permission.
 116

 117 Study selection


 118 All search results were downloaded into an electronic citation manager (Mendeley 1.15.3, 2008-2015

 119 Mendeley Ltd.) and duplicates were removed. When studies had an overlap in player population, the




Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
 120 study with the largest population was included. All remaining titles and abstracts were independently

 121 screened by two reviewers (WD, MM). Full text articles were evaluated for inclusion independently

 122 by two authors (WD, MM). In case of disagreement, consensus was sought through discussion among

 123 the two authors. If no consensus was reached, a third author (JT) took the final decision.


 124


 125 Data extraction


 126 Two authors (WD, HP) extracted data from included studies using a data extraction form adapted from

 127 the Cochrane Collaboration.15 Study authors were contacted in case of missing information. For


 6
  128 randomised controlled trials, only data from the control (i.e. not receiving intervention) group were

 129 extracted.


 130 We extracted: study design, sample size, follow up time, the number of recurrent hamstring injuries12,

 131 definition of hamstring/posterior thigh injury, mean age, sex, competition level (amateur, professional)

 132 and primary outcomes (I. Incidence in n/1000 playing hours. II. proportion of hamstring injuries out of

 133 the total number of injuries). All numeric data were extracted. Where calculations were made to derive

 134 data, a third author (MW) checked the calculations.




Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
 135


 136 Quality assessment


 137 Two authors assessed the study quality (WD, HP) using a modified Newcastle Ottawa Scale for cohort

 138 studies with a seven-star maximum (see Appendix 2).15 Modifications included adding an observation

 139 domain and more focus on injury registration. The following four domains were appraised for quality




Downloaded from www.jospt.org at Ohio State University on December 15, 2020. For personal use only. No other uses without permission.
 140 of reporting:


 141 1. Selection: one star for description of population; one star for recruitment of population, and

 142 one star for description of baseline health and injury status.


 143 2. Observation: one star for surveillance methods and one star when time of observation was

 144 clear.




Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
 145 3. Outcome: one star for accurate and clear definition of acute hamstring injuries or “acute injury

 146 to the posterior thigh”.


 147 4. Other: one star for appropriate other methods.


 148 If no consensus was reached following discussion, a third author (MM) made the final decision.


 149


 150 Data synthesis




 7
  151 Quantitative analysis was precluded due to methodological heterogeneity in the definition of soccer

 152 season, the start of the study in the calendar year and duration of data collection. Instead, we

 153 conducted a descriptive synthesis (see Table 1).


 154 Hamstring incidence was synthesized according to the following subgroups; injury definition, level of

 155 play and sex. We planned grouping findings according to study quality.


 156


 157 Certainty of the evidence (GRADE)




Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
 158 The Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) was used to

 159 appraise the certainty of the evidence.16 Evidence for each incidence measure was assessed. Evidence

 161 at the ‘moderate certainty’ level as recommended for non-randomised study designs. Two authors

 162 (WD, MW) independently rated the evidence on the basis of study limitations, inconsistency,

  164 Results


 165 After removal of duplicates, a total of 451 articles were screened based on title and abstract. This

Exit code 1
 243 Three studies prospectively registered injuries as ‘recurrent’ when another acute hamstring injury in
 244 the same leg occurred during the prospective study period. 5,6,18 All of these studies used the definition
 245 as described in the 2006 consensus 12(box 1). One study6 recorded early (<2 months) recurrences, one
 246 study18 had two groups with early and late (2-12 months) recurrences and one study5 differentiated
 247 between early, late and delayed (>12 months) recurrence. Data were unavailable in one study with
 248 registration of early and late recurrent injuries.18 Overall recurrence ranged from 17% to 34%. 5,6 Early
 249 recurrences ranged from 8% to 17%.
Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
 12
  250 Discussion
 251
 252 We evaluated the incidence, the relative percentage and recurrence rate of acute hamstring injuries in
 253 adult soccer. The incidence of acute hamstring injuries across more than 3868 players in thirteen
 254 included studies ranged from 0.3 to 1.9 injuries per 1000 exposure hours. In women, the incidence was
 255 0.3-0.5 injuries per 1000 exposure hours;19,23 in men the incidence was 0.3-1.9 injuries per 1000
 256 exposure hours. 1,4,28,29,5,6,9,18–21,23 Acute hamstring injuries account for 5 to 15% of all injuries in
 257 soccer.1,4,9,18,19,23,29 The recurrence rate of hamstring injuries was 4% to 68%. These data were
 258 heterogenous and should be interpreted with caution.
 259 Possible explanations for the substantial heterogeneity in hamstring injury incidence are variations in
 260 injury definitions, diverse approaches for observing and registering hamstring injuries, and
 261 methodological shortcomings in the approach to injury surveillance. We rated down the certainty of
 262 the evidence to very low for most incidence measures on the basis of study limitations and
 263 inconsistency.
 264
 265 Shortcomings in the field of research on hamstring injuries
 266 We noted limitations in the planning, conduct and reporting of hamstring studies. We highlight the
 267 most pressing issues here, and provide guidance for future studies on how to conduct better research,
Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
 268 and why this is important.
 269 • Lack of definition of hamstring injury
 270 What constitutes an acute hamstring injury is rarely reported. Only three12,20,28 out of thirteen studies
 271 clearly and comprehensively defined all aspects of the acute hamstring injury. Most of the studies
 272 lacked a description of the character of commencement of the hamstring injury, acute or non-acute.
 273 Acute hamstring injury27 and the non-acute overuse hamstring injury14 are two different types of
 274 injuries with a different etiology, presentation and prognosis. We included acute hamstring injuries
 275 only. Authors were contacted when the character of the hamstring injury was unclear; we were able to
 13
  276 include four more studies, resulting in thirteen inclusions.6,9,19,21. We did not award a star on item 6;
 277 ‘case definition’ for these studies during quality assessment.
 278 • Variation of injury definition in the included studies
 279 Injury definitions varied across studies, with ‘time loss’ used in ten studies’1,5,6,9,18–20,23,29 and ‘tissue’
 280 injury’ in 3 studies4,21,28. ‘Tissue injury is a physical complaint, while ‘time loss’ injury definition is
 281 only registered when this complaint leads to time loss in play. Using ‘tissue’ injury definition could
 282 lead to over-registration of the number of hamstring injuries. Minor soreness not affecting the ability
 283 to play counts as an injury. However, without registration of ‘tissue’ injury definition, the burden of
 284 injury can be underestimated. Being able to play with an injury does not equal being uninjured. Injury
 285 incidence for the studies using the definition ‘tissue’ injury was within the range of incidence for the
 286 included studies using the definition of ‘time loss’ injury.
 287
 288 • Variation in registration of recurrent injuries among included studies
 289 Methods for registering recurrent acute hamstring injuries was a source of variation in the design and
 290 conduct of studies in the field. To reliably register the incidence of hamstring injuries, it is important

296 Ten 1,4–6,18–21,28,29 out of thirteen studies (77%) registered recurrent injuries. Information on injuries
 297 before start of the study was used in seven studies1,4,19–21,28,29 to identify recurrent injuries. However,
 298 bias may be introduced when these data are collected retrospectively, especially when these data are
 299 obtained from the players without medical injury registration. Three studies5,6,18 started scoring
 300 recurrences after an index injury during the study. Hence, first-time injuries in this study may be a mix
 301 index injuries and recurrent injuries.
 14
  302 The lack of registration of injuries occurring prior to the trial period, may overestimate first-time
 303 injuries and underestimate recurrences. Thus, both methods may introduce bias. Future studies must
 304 employ measures to ensure homogeneity in definition and methodology in studies across the field of
 305 acute hamstring injuries. Studies in the field can then be compared and pooled in a meta-analysis.
 306 Another source of heterogenicity was the duration of registration of recurrent injuries. One study6
 307 defined a recurrent injury only when this hamstring injury occurred within two months after the index
 308 injury, the early recurrence. This will underestimate the recurrence rate and overestimate the primary
 309 acute hamstring injury. Others4,5,18–21,28,29 scored recurrent injuries for a longer period, including late
 310 (2-12 months) and delayed recurrences (beyond twelve months). Besides a more accurate incidence
 311 rate on primary and recurrent hamstring injuries, registration in these specific groups will give
 312 valuable information for risk at different points in times for return to sport.
 313
 314 Strengths and Limitations
 315 We used a sensitive search strategy without restriction in language or year of publication and well-
 316 defined inclusion criteria. A large proportion of the literature on acute hamstring injuries has been
 317 excluded. Studies were excluded for not reporting exposure hours, expressing exposure in ‘Athlete
 318 Exposure’ and clustering injuries according to body part (i.e. ‘upper leg’ or ‘thigh’) without
 319 specification to the muscle group (i.e. ‘hamstring’ or ‘posterior thigh’). Whenever ‘hamstring injury’
 320 was not specified to acute or when non-acute or recurrent or data were missing, the author was
 321 contacted by mail to obtain the correct numbers on exposure and the acute hamstring injury. If studies
 322 did not fulfill the eligibility criteria, or when no information on exposures and acute hamstring injuries
 323 could be obtained, studies were excluded. Including these data would have provided a challenge to the
 324 interpretation of the incidence of acute hamstring injuries, the extrapolation of results to other
 325 populations and interstudy comparison.
 15
  326 Study quality assessment was adjusted to the observational research questions of this review, using a
 327 modified Newcastle Ottawa Scale. Adjustments focused on methodologic quality, making this tool a
 328 more appropriate quality assessment for this specific review compared to the original version.
 329 We contacted the lead author of one of the studies21 to obtain data on exposure hours. With these data,
 330 we calculated injury incidence for acute hamstring injuries. For our epidemiological approach, we
 331 excluded players with missing exposure data from the analysis, whereas in the original trial, exposure
 332 hours were analysed on the basis of the intention-to-treat principle. Therefore, the incidence we
 333 calculated for this study was slightly lower than reported in the original report (0.5 vs 0.8,
 334 respectively).
 335 A secondary research question was added after the protocol of the study appeared online, on the
 336 incidence of recurrent acute hamstring injuries. No other changes occurred.
 337 Our review is limited by the number of studies (N=13) and heterogeneous methods across original
 338 studies, hampering a quantitative analysis of the incidence of acute hamstring injuries in soccer. This
 339 is an example that underpins the importance of common methodologies and clear definitions. In
 340 attempt to raise the inclusion rate, authors of eligible studies with missing data, e.g. exposure hours,
 341 were contacted by email. With a low response rate and lack of registration of exposure hours, the
 342 majority of these studies were excluded.
 343 We excluded retrospective studies, limiting the amount of data. Excluding retrospective designs
 344 minimizes risk of bias, and it adheres to a consensus statement for the prospective data collection in
 345 soccer.12
 346 Unpublished data on injury surveillance could be missing. Professional teams and leagues often
 347 register injury data without the intention to publish these data. It is unknown how many teams keep
 348 these registrations, and we have not searched for these data (grey literature).
 349
 350 Five recommendations for future research
 16
  351 Observations from this systematic review stress the importance of a standardized approach to
 352 assessing the incidence of acute hamstring injuries.

 "sourceFile":"Initial assessment and management of select musculoskeletal injuries - A Team Physician Consensus Statement - 2024.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",

 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"The PDF title 'Initial Assessment and Management of Select Musculoskeletal Injuries: A Team Physician Consensus Statement' (Herring et al.) matches the filename and the Crossref title.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Consensus / Position Statement",
 "primaryDomain":"Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains":["Sports Medicine & Injury","Rehabilitation & Return to Sport"],
 "audiences":["Sports Medicine","Athletic Training","Rehabilitation","Performance"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Consensus statement from the Team Physician Consensus Conference, a six-organization project, written by 14 authors for team physicians caring for athletes from youth to Olympic level. It covers initial assessment and management of shoulder dislocation, the disabled throwing shoulder, ulnar collateral ligament tear, hamstring injury, ACL tear, meniscus tear, ankle sprain, groin pain and femoroacetabular impingement, and hip and groin apophyseal injury, using essential and desirable statements. The authors state that nonoperative care is the usual first step for most of these injuries and that multimodal prevention programs reduce ACL and hamstring injury incidence.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The statement is explicitly not a standard of care, applies no systematic review, and gives no evidence levels or recommendation grades. It covers only select injuries, so many common presentations are outside its scope.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could treat these statements as a standard of care or as graded recommendations, when the authors say neither applies.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2024,
   "citation":"Herring SA, Kibler WB, Putukian M, Boyajian-O'Neill LA, Chang CJ, Franks RR, et al. Initial Assessment and Management of Select Musculoskeletal Injuries: A Team Physician Consensus Statement. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2024;23(3):86-104.",
   "doi":"10.1249/jsr.0000000000001151",
   "abstract":"The Team Physician Consensus Conference summarizes initial assessment and management of select musculoskeletal injuries in athletes. Each topic covers mechanism, clinical presentation, evaluation, nonoperative and operative options and injury risk modification, with statements labelled essential or desirable.",
   "tldr":"This is a practical reference for the first assessment and early management of shoulder dislocation, UCL, hamstring, ACL, meniscus, ankle, groin and apophyseal injuries. It is a consensus guide rather than a graded evidence review, so check specific decisions against current literature.",
   "methods":"Expert consensus. An executive committee selected topics and drafted an outline, representatives of six professional organizations reviewed the literature for each topic, and statements were agreed by unanimous consensus at in-person meetings before board approval. The statement was co-published in Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise (2024;56(3):385-401). No systematic review, levels of evidence or recommendation grades were included.",
   "findings":"Each topic lists essential information every team physician should know and desirable information for ideal settings. Nonoperative care is the initial approach for most disabled throwing shoulder and UCL presentations and most hamstring injuries, with surgery reserved for failed or high-demand cases. The statement reports that multimodal prevention programs reduce ACL and hamstring injury, that eccentric strength training reduces hamstring injury risk, and that core stabilizing exercise reduces load and injury risk.",
   "limitations":"The authors state that the statement is not a standard of care and is general in nature, that only select topics are included, and that no systematic review or evidence grading was done. Several sections note limited high-quality evidence, including for biologic and corticosteroid injections, stretching as a risk modifier, and the value of biologic therapy for UCL injury.",
   "practicalImplications":"Use the essential points as a first-assessment checklist: confirm the mechanism, examine neurovascular status, obtain the imaging named for each injury, and set referral criteria. Treat the surgical indications as triggers for referral rather than default plans.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: the workload and kinetic-chain sections, which cover monitoring load and screening the whole kinetic chain for throwing shoulder and UCL injury, can guide load planning for throwers. The statement names eccentric strength and core work as the main hamstring risk-modification items.",
   "rtp":"Return to Sport Application: the statement treats return to play as an individualized decision. It says most athletes out of overhead sport after UCL reconstruction are out for 12 months or longer and that throwers need a specific throwing protocol before return. It does not give return timelines for most injuries, so use the injury-specific criteria in the full text."
 }

 "audiences":["Nutrition","Sports Medicine","Performance","Athletic Training"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Narrative review of studies of intermittent fasting, including Ramadan fasting, time-restricted eating and alternate-day fasting, across high-intensity, endurance and resistance exercise. Most cited studies are small crossover or observational studies in footballers, cyclists, rowers or resistance-trained men, plus one mouse study. The authors report mixed results, with some studies showing reduced sprint, cycling, rowing or endurance performance and others showing no effect, and no study showing a performance benefit.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The review describes no search strategy or inclusion criteria, and its evidence is mostly small studies and Ramadan fasting, which also changes sleep and fluid intake. The authors also define the 5:2 diet inconsistently between the Introduction (alternating days) and the Discussion (5 days fasting, 2 days eating).",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read 'no benefit' as proof that intermittent fasting harms performance, when the authors describe mixed results from mostly small, short-term studies.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2019,
   "citation":"Levy E, Chu T. Intermittent Fasting and Its Effects on Athletic Performance: A Review. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2019;18(7):266-269.",
   "doi":"10.1249/jsr.0000000000000614",
   "abstract":"The authors review studies on intermittent fasting and athletic performance across high-intensity, endurance and resistance exercise. Most data come from Ramadan fasting and overnight fasts. They report varied outcomes, with no study showing an improvement in performance, and call for long-term studies of specific fasting protocols.",
   "tldr":"Intermittent fasting does not appear to improve athletic performance and may impair sprint, cycling, rowing or endurance output in some studies. Athletes who fast should track their performance on fasting and fed days, and current data do not support fasting as a rapid weight-loss method before weigh-ins.",
   "methods":"Narrative review of published studies, grouped by exercise type (high-intensity, endurance and resistance) and by fasting type (Ramadan, time-restricted and alternate-day). The authors cite a 2018 systematic review of fasted-state exercise, but no search method or selection criteria are described for this review.",
   "findings":"In Ramadan studies, several showed small, non-significant decreases in sprint performance, and one study of Algerian footballers reported a 16% decrease in endurance capacity. In a 2019 crossover study of ten rowers, omitting breakfast impaired evening 2000 m time-trial performance, and cyclists who skipped breakfast had lower evening performance. Resistance training studies over 8 weeks found little or no harm to lean mass or strength, although one reported lower testosterone and IGF-1 at 8 weeks.",
   "limitations":"The authors note varied definitions of fasting, varied outcome measures, small samples, and few studies of the specific 5:2 and 16:8 regimens. Ramadan studies confound fasting with sleep disruption and dehydration, and the mouse work may not transfer to humans.",
   "practicalImplications":"Athletes who adopt intermittent fasting should track sprint, cycling or time-trial output on fasting and fed days, because impairments appeared in several studies. Coaches should not expect intermittent fasting to improve performance, and current data do not support its use for rapid weight loss in weight-class sports.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: if an athlete fasts, log high-intensity and endurance output across fasting and fed days, since the review found impairments and no benefit. Resistance training appeared less affected, though the studies were short.",
   "rtp":"Return to Sport Application: the review does not address injury or return to sport and cannot inform return-to-play decisions."
 }
}

{
 "id":"Q24",
 "sourceFile":"Ischemic strength training - a low load alternative to     heavy resistance exercise.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"The PDF title 'Ischemic Strength Training: A Low-Load Alternative to Heavy Resistance Exercise?' (Wernbom, Augustsson and Raastad, Scandinavian Journal of Medicine and Science in Sports proof) matches the filename and the Crossref title.",
 "confidence":"medium",
 "studyDesign":"Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain":"Training & Performance",
 "domains":["Training & Performance","Rehabilitation & Return to Sport"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Rehabilitation","Athletic Training","Research & Analytics"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Narrative review of strength training combined with vascular occlusion (ischemic or Kaatsu training), covering motor unit recruitment, hormones, growth factors, safety, cuff width and dose. The authors cite 13 training studies with 116 subjects, mostly untrained or physically active adults, in which low-load training with a cuff produced strength and muscle size gains comparable to heavy training in several studies. They conclude the method appears relatively safe in the short term, but the mechanisms are unclear and tendon and possibly neural adaptations appear smaller than with heavy training.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The review states it summarizes current opinion and describes no search method, so study selection cannot be reproduced. Most evidence comes from 2 to 8 week studies, with two of 16 weeks, and much of the safety data comes from a national survey published by the same research group.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could assume that low-load cuff training matches heavy lifting for every goal, when the paper reports smaller tendon and possibly neural effects and most gains came from sets taken to or near failure.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2008,
   "citation":"Wernbom M, Augustsson J, Raastad T. Ischemic Strength Training: A Low-Load Alternative to Heavy Resistance Exercise? Scandinavian Journal of Medicine and Science in Sports. 2008.",
   "doi":"10.1111/j.1600-0838.2008.00788.x",
   "abstract":"The authors review the physiology, safety and dosing of strength training combined with vascular occlusion. They note that low-load occlusion training produces strength and size gains comparable to heavy training in several studies, but that mechanisms, long-term safety and practical use remain unclear. They suggest that relative ischemia may occur without a cuff at some loads.",
   "tldr":"Low-load training with a tourniquet can build muscle and strength, but the mechanisms, long-term safety and practical dose are unresolved. Where heavy loads are contraindicated, it is an option, with wide cuffs at lower pressures preferred and attention to soreness and effort.",
   "methods":"Narrative review of the authors' and published work on motor unit recruitment, hormonal and local growth factor responses, safety, cuff width and training dose. The authors summarize 13 training studies in Table 1, but no search strategy or inclusion criteria are described.",
   "findings":"Low-load training with partial occlusion at about 20% to 50% of 1RM produced muscle size and strength gains comparable to heavy training in several studies. In one study, a low-load occlusion leg and a high-load leg gained similar quadriceps volume, but only the high-load leg increased tendon-aponeurosis stiffness. A Japanese survey of more than 12,600 occlusion-training users reported subcutaneous hemorrhage in 13.1% and rare serious events, including venous thrombosis in 0.055%.",
   "limitations":"The authors state that long-term safety, soft-tissue effects, optimal frequency and whether cuffs add benefit beyond effort need further study. Several supporting points rest on unpublished observations, and one partial-occlusion cycling study (Eiken et al.) found an 8% fall in peak torque despite fiber-area gains.",
   "practicalImplications":"If a cuff is used, the authors favor relatively wide cuffs at lower pressures, noting about 90 to 110 mm Hg was enough in their unpublished observations, rather than high pressures with narrow cuffs. Expect intense muscle pain and delayed soreness, which the authors say lessens with low starting volumes of 1 to 2 sets, and note that the training demands high motivation.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: the review supports low-load occlusion as a complement to strength work or when heavy loads are inappropriate. It does not show it beats heavy training for tendon or neural adaptation, so do not use it to replace heavy lifting for strength-focused athletes.",
   "rtp":"Return to Sport Application: the review is aimed at rehabilitation where heavy forces are contraindicated, but it gives no return-to-play criteria and no injured-athlete trials. Any use should be under clinical oversight, since the authors call soft-tissue and safety effects unresolved."
 }
}

37	forces acting upon the musculoskeletal system are contraindicated. Several studies on low to
38	moderate-intensity resistance exercise combined with cuff occlusion have demonstrated
39	increases in muscle strength and size that are comparable to those typically seen after
40	conventional high-load strength training. However, the physiological mechanisms by which
41	occlusion training induces increased muscle mass and strength are currently unclear, although
42	several candidate stimuli have been proposed. Also, the long-term safety, practicality and
43	efficacy of this training method are still controversial. Furthermore, recent studies have
44	demonstrated that in some instances, tourniquet cuffs may not be necessary for relative
45	ischemia and significant training effects to occur with resistance exercise at low to moderate
46	loads. The aims of the present review are to summarize current opinion and knowledge
47	 regarding the physiology of ischemic strength training and to discuss some of the training and
48	health aspects of this type of exercise. In addition, suggestions for further research are given.

50	Strength training is an important component of training in most sports as well as in the area of
51	 injury prevention and rehabilitation (Escamilla & Wickham, 2003). In the prescription of
52	resistance exercise, training intensity or the load used is commonly regarded as the most
53	important variable (Fleck & Kraemer, 1997). The intensity in dynamic resistance training is
54	often quantified as a function of the maximum weight that can be lifted only once (one
55	repetition maximum, 1RM). Most authors agree that the load should be at least 60% of 1RM
56	in order to stimulate increases in strength and that optimal strength gains results from loads in
57	excess of 80% of 1RM (Atha, 1981; Häkkinen, 1994; Fleck & Kraemer, 1997; ACSM, 2002;
58	Andersen et al, 2006). For muscle hypertrophy, loads of 6-12RM are usually recommended,
59	corresponding to ~70-85% of 1RM (Häkkinen, 1994; Fleck & Kraemer, 1997; ACSM, 2002).
60	In the clinical setting, however, it is often difficult and sometimes also contraindicated
61	to use near-maximal loads (e.g. early rehabilitation after a sports injury). Muscle atrophy and
62	 weakness often occur rapidly in the affected area due to the effects of trauma (or disease) and
63	inactivity. Consequently, training modalities that promote hypertrophy or counteract atrophy
64	 without the use of heavy loads should be of special interest in the rehabilitation of injuries and
65	some chronic diseases for which high musculoskeletal forces are contraindicated.
66	In the mid 1990’s, Rooney et al. (1994) and Schott et al. (1995) suggested that fatigue
67	and metabolite accumulation were important factors in the resistance exercise stimulus
68	leading to increased strength and accretion of muscle mass. These findings were extended by
69	Shinohara et al. (1998) and Takarada et al. (2000b), who used tourniquet cuffs to partially
70	restrict the muscle blood flow during training with low resistance in order to cause increases
71	in muscle strength. In these and in several subsequent studies (Takarada et al., 2002, 2004;
72	Burgomaster et al., 2003; Abe et al, 2005a, b; Kubo et al., 2006) low to moderate intensity
73	 (20-50% of 1RM) resistance training with vascular occlusion has been shown to lead to gains
74	in muscle strength and volume comparable to those seen after conventional heavy resistance
75	training. In one recent study, hypertrophy of the quadriceps was even observed after walk
76	training with tourniquets (Abe et al., 2006). It has also been reported that brief intermittent
77	 tourniquet-induced ischemia-reperfusion, without exercise, can decrease disuse atrophy; at
78	least in some muscles (Takarada et al., 2000c; Clark et al., 2006, Kubota et al., 2008).

 Exercise?
 Journal: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine and Science in Sports
 Manuscript ID: draft
 Manuscript Type: Review

 Author:
Complete List of Authors: Wernbom, Mathias; Lundberg laboratory for human muscle function
 and movement analysis, Department of orthopaedics
 Strength training, Ischemia , Vascular occlusion, Muscle
 Keywords:
 hypertrophy, Muscle atrophy
 Ischemic Strength Training: A Low-Load
 Alternative to Heavy Resistance Exercise?
M. Wernbom1, J. Augustsson1, T. Raastad2
1. Lundberg Laboratory for Human Muscle Function and Movement Analysis,
Department of Orthopaedics, the Sahlgrenska Academy at Göteborg University,
 Göteborg, Sweden
2. Department of Physical Performance, Norwegian School of Sport Sciences, Oslo,
Norway.
Corresponding author:
Mathias Wernbom
 Lundberg Laboratory for Human Muscle Function & Movement Analysis
Department of Orthopaedics
Gröna Stråket 12
Sahlgrenska University Hospital
SE-413 45 Göteborg, Sweden
 E-mail: mathias.wernbom@orthop.gu.se
 Fax: +46 31 416816
 Phone: +46 31 426891
 Key words: strength training, ischemia, vascular occlusion, muscle hypertrophy, muscle
atrophy
 Abstract
Strength training with low loads in combination with vascular occlusion has been proposed as
 an alternative to heavy resistance exercise in the rehabilitation setting, especially when high
forces acting upon the musculoskeletal system are contraindicated. Several studies on low to
moderate-intensity resistance exercise combined with cuff occlusion have demonstrated
increases in muscle strength and size that are comparable to those typically seen after
conventional high-load strength training. However, the physiological mechanisms by which
occlusion training induces increased muscle mass and strength are currently unclear, although
several candidate stimuli have been proposed. Also, the long-term safety, practicality and
efficacy of this training method are still controversial. Furthermore, recent studies have
demonstrated that in some instances, tourniquet cuffs may not be necessary for relative
ischemia and significant training effects to occur with resistance exercise at low to moderate
loads. The aims of the present review are to summarize current opinion and knowledge
 regarding the physiology of ischemic strength training and to discuss some of the training and
health aspects of this type of exercise. In addition, suggestions for further research are given.
 Introduction
Strength training is an important component of training in most sports as well as in the area of
 injury prevention and rehabilitation (Escamilla & Wickham, 2003). In the prescription of
resistance exercise, training intensity or the load used is commonly regarded as the most
important variable (Fleck & Kraemer, 1997). The intensity in dynamic resistance training is
often quantified as a function of the maximum weight that can be lifted only once (one
repetition maximum, 1RM). Most authors agree that the load should be at least 60% of 1RM
in order to stimulate increases in strength and that optimal strength gains results from loads in
excess of 80% of 1RM (Atha, 1981; Häkkinen, 1994; Fleck & Kraemer, 1997; ACSM, 2002;
Andersen et al, 2006). For muscle hypertrophy, loads of 6-12RM are usually recommended,
corresponding to ~70-85% of 1RM (Häkkinen, 1994; Fleck & Kraemer, 1997; ACSM, 2002).
In the clinical setting, however, it is often difficult and sometimes also contraindicated
to use near-maximal loads (e.g. early rehabilitation after a sports injury). Muscle atrophy and
 weakness often occur rapidly in the affected area due to the effects of trauma (or disease) and
inactivity. Consequently, training modalities that promote hypertrophy or counteract atrophy
 without the use of heavy loads should be of special interest in the rehabilitation of injuries and
some chronic diseases for which high musculoskeletal forces are contraindicated.
In the mid 1990’s, Rooney et al. (1994) and Schott et al. (1995) suggested that fatigue
and metabolite accumulation were important factors in the resistance exercise stimulus
leading to increased strength and accretion of muscle mass. These findings were extended by
Shinohara et al. (1998) and Takarada et al. (2000b), who used tourniquet cuffs to partially
restrict the muscle blood flow during training with low resistance in order to cause increases
in muscle strength. In these and in several subsequent studies (Takarada et al., 2002, 2004;
Burgomaster et al., 2003; Abe et al, 2005a, b; Kubo et al., 2006) low to moderate intensity
 (20-50% of 1RM) resistance training with vascular occlusion has been shown to lead to gains
in muscle strength and volume comparable to those seen after conventional heavy resistance
training. In one recent study, hypertrophy of the quadriceps was even observed after walk
training with tourniquets (Abe et al., 2006). It has also been reported that brief intermittent
 tourniquet-induced ischemia-reperfusion, without exercise, can decrease disuse atrophy; at
least in some muscles (Takarada et al., 2000c; Clark et al., 2006, Kubota et al., 2008).
The combination of low loads and large training effects suggests that ischemic strength
 training may be a useful method in rehabilitation and other contexts. However, the practicality
and the safety of training with vascular occlusion remain controversial. Therefore, the purpose
of the present review is to summarize current opinion and knowledge regarding the
physiology of ischemic strength training and to discuss some of the training and health
aspects of this type of exercise.
Physiology
Motor unit recruitment
 It is generally believed that only muscle fibers that are activated during exercise grow as a
result of strength training (Kraemer, Fleck & Evans, 1996). The size principle of motor unit
recruitment dictates that small units composed of slow but fatigue resistant fibers are recruited
first and with increasing demands for force or power, ever larger units are recruited
