 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Narrative review of actigraphy and consumer sleep wearable studies in athletes and non-athletes, which the authors state is more narrative than structured. Wearables detect sleep reasonably well but are weaker at detecting wake, with wake accuracy of about 49% to 60% in validation studies. The authors report that proprietary summary sleep scores have no identified link to training, performance or recovery.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The review describes no search or selection method and presents no new data. The authors note that the field has few studies, many of them industry sponsored, so the review cannot show whether wearable sleep data change performance or recovery outcomes.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read a consumer sleep score as a validated measure of recovery, when the authors state its clinical meaning is unknown.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2025,
   "citation":"Kaufman MW, Shetty M, Nguyen C, Abas J, Fredericson M, Zeitzer J. Focused Review of Sleep Wearable Technology and Its Application in Sports Performance. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2025;24(6):171-176.",
   "doi":"10.1249/jsr.0000000000001258",
   "abstract":"The authors review the history, accuracy and current use of sleep wearables, which are mostly wrist-worn actigraphs. They conclude that wearables detect sleep reasonably well but struggle to separate quiet wakefulness from early sleep, and that proprietary sleep scores are not yet clinically interpretable for athletes.",
   "tldr":"Sleep wearables can show sleep trends across a season, but their summary scores have not been linked to training, performance or recovery. When the device and the athlete's own sense of sleep disagree, the athlete's report should take priority.",
   "methods":"Narrative review of published actigraphy validation studies and athlete sleep studies. The authors state the review is more narrative than structured because device validity depends on hardware and software that can change.",
   "findings":"Wearables show high sensitivity for detecting sleep but poor sensitivity for detecting wake, with wake accuracy of about 49% to 60% in validation studies. Actigraphy agreed with polysomnography at 81% to 90% in elite athletes in the cited work. No study has linked a consumer summary sleep score to training, performance or recovery outcomes.",
   "limitations":"The authors acknowledge that the review is not structured, that many validation studies are industry sponsored, and that device algorithms are proprietary. The paper presents no original data.",
   "practicalImplications":"Use wearables to see sleep trends across a season and around travel or schedule changes, but do not treat a summary sleep score as a clinical result. Keep clinical presentation and subjective report as the basis for decisions.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: track sleep trends across a season, including travel, to see how schedule changes line up with training and recovery. Do not set sleep-score targets for athletes, since the score's link to performance is unestablished.",
   "rtp":"Return to Sport Application: the review suggests wearables may help detect sleep disturbances that can accompany concussion, but it states they are likely not sensitive or specific and are not a substitute for clinical presentation. Clinical examination and the athlete's report should guide decisions."
 },
 "verification":{
   "status":"CORRECTED",
   "changes":[
     "screeningLimitations: 'Most validation work is industry sponsored, and few studies are athlete-specific' overstated the text -> now 'few studies, many of them industry sponsored' ('there are currently few research studies, and many of these are done with industry sponsorship')"
   ],
   "residualConcerns":"The rtp field touches concussion detection; the paper only says wearables 'represent an opportunity' and are 'likely not sensitive or specific', so it must not be cited as support for wearable-based concussion screening.",
   "spotCheckPriority":"high"
 }
}

{
 "id":"Q18",
 "sourceFile":"Height restrictions for dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry - What are our options for body composition and bone health precision.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"The PDF title 'Height Restrictions for Dual-energy X-ray Absorptiometry: What Are Our Options for Body Composition and Bone Health Precision?' (Redinger et al.) matches the filename and the Crossref title.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Methodological / Validation Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Monitoring & Technology",
 "domains":["Monitoring & Technology","Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences":["Research & Analytics","Athletic Training","Performance","Sports Medicine"],
 "sports":["Basketball","American Football","Volleyball"],
 "populations":["Adult / Recreational"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Cross-sectional DXA precision study of 60 adults (34.8 +/- 11.9 years; 30 men and 30 women; mean BMI 26) who had three total-body scans on a GE Lunar Prodigy (n = 15) or Hologic Horizon A (n = 45), with one GE Lunar iDXA used for exploratory analysis. A combined scan built from an upper-body region of the head-first scan and a lower-body region of the flipped scan added 0.25% to 0.63% error on the Lunar Prodigy, but added about 4.35% BMC error on the Horizon A and 3.71% BMC error on the iDXA.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The sample was non-athlete adults who were all shorter than 193 cm, so the method was not tested on athletes who actually exceed the table. The iDXA result comes from one participant and is exploratory.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the combined-scan method as a precise way to track any tall athlete on any DXA model, when the bone mineral content error was large on the newer Hologic and GE units.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2024,
   "citation":"Redinger AL, Russell JL, Allen SMF, Baker BS. Height Restrictions for Dual-energy X-ray Absorptiometry: What Are Our Options for Body Composition and Bone Health Precision? Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2024.",
   "doi":"10.1519/jsc.0000000000004775",
   "abstract":"Sixty adults were scanned three times on GE Lunar Prodigy or Hologic Horizon A DXA units, and a combined upper and lower body region of interest was built from a flipped scan. The combined scan added less than 1% error on the Lunar Prodigy but added large bone mineral content error on the newer Hologic and GE units.",
   "tldr":"On older GE Lunar Prodigy systems, a combined-region scan keeps body composition precise for athletes who exceed the table height, with less than 1% added error. On newer Hologic and GE units, the combined method makes bone mineral content too unreliable for serial comparison, so use the same landmarks and region heights.",
   "methods":"Cross-sectional precision study. Participants completed two identical total-body scans and one flipped total-body scan, analysed by trained technicians using ISCD guidance. Coefficient of variation, paired t tests, Cohen d, Pearson r and Bland-Altman analysis compared baseline scans with the combined-region scans.",
   "findings":"On the Lunar Prodigy, the combined-region scan changed precision by 0.25% (bone-free lean mass) to 0.63% (fat mass), with a significant but trivial bone mineral content difference (p = 0.002, d = 0.10). On the Hologic Horizon A, bone mineral content error rose by 4.35% (CV 0.80% to 5.15%), fat mass by 0.31% and bone-free lean mass by less than 0.01%; the BMC and fat mass differences were significant but with trivial effect sizes. On the iDXA, the authors report 3.71% bone mineral content, 4.80% lean mass and 7.39% fat mass error from a single participant.",
   "limitations":"The participants were non-athletes who fit on the table, and the iDXA result is from one person. The analysis comes from one lab with trained technicians, and the study does not test athletes above the table height limit directly.",
   "practicalImplications":"Labs with older Lunar Prodigy units can use the combined-region method for serial assessment of tall athletes, after checking baseline precision. Labs with newer Hologic or GE units should instead use the shortest common region of interest across all scans and keep the same bony landmarks, because the combined method adds large bone error.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: athletes taller than the table limit (about 193 cm) can be tracked with the combined-region scan on an older Lunar Prodigy, or with the shortest common region on newer units, as long as the same landmarks and region heights are used over time. Do not compare body composition across scans that cut different body segments.",
   "rtp":"Return to Sport Application: the study does not address return to sport. Bone-mineral trends from scans with altered or omitted regions should not be used to judge bone recovery or injury risk in tall athletes."
 },
 "verification":{
   "status":"CORRECTED",
   "changes":[
     "paper.findings: Horizon A soft-tissue values were garbled ('fat mass and lean mass changed by less than 0.5% and 0.31%') -> FM +0.31%, BFLBM <0.01%, BMC +4.35% from 0.80% to 5.15% (Table 2: 'BMC 0.80% 5.15%', 'BFLBM 0.48% 0.48% <0.01%', 'FM 0.95% 1.26% 0.31%')",
     "paper.limitations: removed the extraction-artifact note about '14.35%' (moved to residualConcerns, it is not a study limitation)",
     "paper.athleteDev: implied the combined scan works on any unit -> combined scan only on the Lunar Prodigy, shortest common region on newer units ('newer DXA systems cannot use the stitched scan technique')",
     "screeningLimitations: added that all participants were shorter than 193 cm ('were shorter than 193 cm. This ensured that subjects would comfortably fit')"
   ],
   "residualConcerns":"The extracted text renders the plus sign as '1', so Table 2 and the Discussion read '14.35%' and '13.71%'; the abstract ('0.01-4.35%') and Table 2 baseline and combined CVs confirm +4.35% and 3.71%. Citation omits volume and pages because the PDF shows only the XX(X):000-000 placeholder.",
   "spotCheckPriority":"normal"
 }
}

 "evidenceSummary":"Online mixed-methods survey of 191 performance support staff (179 men, 12 women) working in professional (n = 147) or international (n = 44) sport, recruited by social media and referral.    "abstract":"A mixed-methods online survey of 191 performance support staff in professional or international sport examined their views on decision-making, how they learn it and how they track decisions. Most rated decision-making as very important, but few had formal training or a formal review process, and staff described pressure, poor team communication and cognitive biases as obstacles.",
   "tldr":"Performance staff rate decision-making as central to their role, yet most have no formal training and no structured way to review key decisions. The authors suggest starting with basic education on decision-making and cognitive bias, then adding a formal process for tracking and reviewing major decisions.",
   "methods":"Nonprobability (purposive and snowball) recruitment over an 8-week period. An online questionnaire with nine decision-making items (eight closed, one open) and six demographic items was checked by a five-expert panel. Closed items were summarized descriptively, and the open item was analysed by thematic analysis.",
   "findings":"Decision-making was rated 5 or higher by 98% of respondents (median 7). Ninety percent believed team decisions give better outcomes than individual decisions. Thirty-one percent had received formal decision-making education, 69% had no formal strategy for scoring key decisions, and 22% consistently reviewed and adjusted plans. Five themes emerged from the open responses: environmental pressures, lack of systems and processes, underdeveloped decision capabilities, dysfunctional team dynamics and cognitive biases.",
   "limitations":"The authors note that the sample was recruited non-randomly, that only 12 respondents were women, and that the findings may not generalize to all professional sport. The survey did not measure the type of decision training received, and the preference for experiential over targeted training (median 3 on a 7-point scale) was not explored further.    "athleteDev":"Performance Application: staff who make training-load, selection or return-related calls can keep a simple log of key decisions and their outcomes and review it on a set schedule. The paper does not test whether this improves decision quality.",

 "decision":"DEGRADED",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"The article's own DOI is not printed in the text, and the externalDoi cannot be used: 10.1016/j.jbmt.2018.09.037 is registered in Crossref to Journal of Bodywork and Movement Therapies 22(4):858, a one-page item with the same title and authors, not this 7-page Journal of Sports Science and Medicine article (2018;17:298-304). No JSSM DOI was found in Crossref.",
 "doiMissing":true,
 "identityCheck":"The PDF is 'Improvement of Functional Ankle Properties Following Supplementation with Specific Collagen Peptides in Athletes with Chronic Ankle Instability' (Dressler et al.), Journal of Sports Science and Medicine 2018;17:298-304, which matches the filename. The Crossref match behind externalDoi is a different publication (JBMT 22(4):858), so the DOI is not this article's own.",
 "confidence":"medium",
 "studyDesign":"Randomized Controlled Trial",
 "primaryDomain":"Nutrition & Hydration",
 "domains":["Nutrition & Hydration","Sports Medicine & Injury","Rehabilitation & Return to Sport"],
 "audiences":["Nutrition","Sports Medicine","Rehabilitation","Athletic Training"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Male Athletes","Female Athletes","Injured Athletes","Adult / Recreational"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 50 amateur athletes with chronic ankle instability (CAIT 24 or lower; mean age about 27), who completed 6 months of 5 g daily specific collagen peptides or maltodextrin placebo plus three weekly home loading sessions. Within the collagen group, CAIT rose by 5.28 points (SEM 1.16, p less than 0.001) while placebo changed by 0.65, and FAAM-G ADL and Sport scores improved more with collagen; ankle stiffness did not differ between groups.",
 "screeningLimitations":"Most outcomes are self-reported, and the 3-month sprain and injury counts are yes/no recall. Baseline CAIT and FAAM-G scores differed significantly between groups, with the collagen group starting lower, and the study was partly funded by the supplier (Gelita AG) with a co-author from the Collagen Research Institute.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the larger CAIT gain as proof that collagen beats placebo, when the collagen group started much lower, finished with a mean CAIT (20.76) still below placebo (21.45) and still in the instability range, and showed no mechanical stiffness effect.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2018,
   "citation":"Dressler P, Gehring D, Zdzieblik D, Oesser S, Gollhofer A, Konig D. Improvement of Functional Ankle Properties Following Supplementation with Specific Collagen Peptides in Athletes with Chronic Ankle Instability. Journal of Sports Science and Medicine. 2018;17:298-304.",
   "doi":"",
   "abstract":"Fifty athletes with chronic ankle instability took 5 g a day of specific collagen peptides or placebo for six months alongside home loading exercise. The collagen group improved on subjective ankle function scores and reported fewer ankle sprains at three months, but ankle stiffness did not differ between groups.",
   "tldr":"In athletes with chronic ankle instability, a daily 5 g collagen peptide supplement improved self-reported ankle function over six months more than placebo. The result rests on self-report and on groups that differed at baseline, and the stiffness measure showed no group difference, so it is a promising but unconfirmed finding.",
   "methods":"Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Sixty athletes were recruited, and 50 completed the 6-month intervention (25 per group) with compliance calendars. Outcomes were CAIT, FAAM-G ADL and Sport, anterior talar drawer stiffness by arthrometer, and a 3-month follow-up questionnaire on sprains, giving way and injuries. Analysis used two-way repeated-measures ANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc tests.",
   "findings":"The collagen group's CAIT rose by 5.28 points (SEM 1.16, p less than 0.001 within group), while placebo changed by 0.65 (not significant); the treatment by time interaction was significant (p less than 0.001), but at 6 months the collagen group's mean CAIT (20.76) was still below placebo (21.45). FAAM-G ADL rose 9.76 and Sport rose 19.88 percentage points in the collagen group, with no change in placebo. At 3 months, 24 of 25 collagen participants answered yes to reduced ankle sprains versus 9 of 25 placebo participants (p less than 0.001). Ankle stiffness did not differ between groups.",
   "limitations":"Baseline CAIT (15.5 versus 20.8) and FAAM-G scores differed significantly between groups, and the authors acknowledge this may have enlarged the collagen effect. Outcomes were self-reported, the 3-month follow-up had no objective measures and no 6-month follow-up, and the authors declare no conflicts while noting supplier cost support and a co-author who directs the Collagen Research Institute. Table 1 lists the ANOVA as p less than 0.05 while the text gives interaction p less than 0.001.",
   "practicalImplications":"Collagen peptides taken within an hour of loading sessions may be worth considering as an adjunct for athletes with chronic instability, given the self-reported gains. Because the stiffness measure did not change and the trial is small and self-reported, it does not support the supplement as a substitute for the neuromuscular, proprioceptive and strength work the authors describe as standard therapy.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: no performance outcome was measured. The relevant use is ankle stability work for athletes with recurrent sprains, where the self-reported gains and sprain counts are early, unconfirmed support for trying the supplement as an adjunct.",
   "rtp":"Return to Sport Application: the trial did not measure return to sport or time loss. Its sprain counts are self-reported, so the result cannot clear an athlete or set a return date."
 },

{
 "id":"Q21",
 "sourceFile":"Incidence of acute hamstring injuries in soccer - A systematic review of 13 studies involving more than 3800 athletes with 2 million sport exposure hours.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"The PDF title 'Incidence of acute hamstring injuries in soccer: A systematic review of 13 studies involving more than 3800 athletes with 2 million sport exposure hours' (Diemer et al.) matches the filename and the Crossref title.",
 "confidence":"medium",
 "studyDesign":"Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain":"Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains":["Sports Medicine & Injury","Monitoring & Technology"],
 "audiences":["Sports Medicine","Athletic Training","Rehabilitation","Research & Analytics","Coaching"],
 "sports":["Soccer"],
 "populations":["Professional / Elite","Adult / Recreational","Male Athletes","Female Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Systematic review (PROSPERO CRD42016039011) of prospective studies in adult soccer players reporting acute hamstring injuries per 1000 exposure hours. Thirteen studies with 3868 players and about 2.07 million exposure hours were included, and the synthesis was descriptive because the studies differed in how they defined the season, when they started and how long they collected data. The authors report 0.3 to 1.9 acute hamstring injuries per 1000 exposure hours, recurrence of 4% to 68%, and certainty of evidence from moderate to very low.",
 "screeningLimitations":"No pooled estimate was calculated, and only two included studies reported women. At full-text review, 51 studies were excluded for lacking hamstring-specific data and 30 for lacking exposure hours, so the findings rest on a narrow evidence base with heterogeneous injury definitions.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could compare these incidence figures directly with their own squad's injury rates, when the included studies used different injury definitions and exposure measures.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2021,
   "citation":"Diemer WM, Winters M, Tol JL, Pas HIMFL, Moen MH. Incidence of acute hamstring injuries in soccer: a systematic review of 13 studies involving more than 3800 athletes with 2 million sport exposure hours. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2021.",
   "doi":"10.2519/jospt.2021.9305",
   "abstract":"Thirteen prospective studies of adult soccer players were summarized descriptively to estimate acute hamstring injury incidence and recurrence. Incidence was 0.3 to 1.9 per 1000 exposure hours, and recurrence ranged from 4% to 68%, with certainty of evidence rated from moderate to very low.",
   "tldr":"Acute hamstring injuries in soccer occur at roughly 0.3 to 1.9 per 1000 exposure hours in training and matches. The wide range reflects inconsistent injury definitions and exposure recording, so compare your own data with these figures only after matching definitions.",
   "methods":"PRISMA-guided systematic review, prospectively registered in PROSPERO. Five databases were searched to August 2019 without language or date limits, and two reviewers screened and extracted data. Eligible studies were prospective, in adult soccer players, and reported acute hamstring injuries with exposure hours. Quality was assessed with a modified Newcastle-Ottawa scale and certainty with GRADE.",
   "findings":"Incidence was 0.4 to 1.9 per 1000 hours with time-loss definitions and 0.3 to 1.0 with tissue-based definitions. Professional players had 0.5 to 1.9 per 1000 hours with time-loss definitions, and women in two studies had 0.3 to 0.5. Acute hamstring injuries made up 5% to 15% of all soccer injuries across seven studies, and recurrence ranged from 4% to 68% depending on the definition and follow-up window. Certainty was very low for most measures, low for women and moderate only for the single-study professional tissue-definition estimate.",
   "limitations":"The authors note the small number of studies, heterogeneous methods, exclusion of studies without exposure hours, and very low certainty for most measures. The abstract and results give 5% to 15% of injuries while the Conclusions and Key Points give 5% to 13%, and the record uses the results value.",
   "practicalImplications":"Use the 0.3 to 1.9 per 1000 hour range as a rough benchmark for how common acute hamstring injuries are in soccer. Record exposure in minutes, code injuries to the muscle group, and state whether a time-loss or tissue definition is used, so that your own surveillance can be compared with published rates.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: the review gives no training intervention. Its use for performance staff is to set up injury surveillance with exposure hours, muscle-specific injury definitions and, where possible, intensity measures, so that squad data can be compared later.",
   "rtp":"Return to Sport Application: the review does not set return-to-play timelines. It reports recurrence of 4% to 68% and notes that recurrence definitions drive those rates, so the figures should be interpreted cautiously and not used alone for return decisions."
 },
 "verification":{
   "status":"CORRECTED",
   "changes":[
     "screeningLimitations: '51 studies were excluded for missing exposure hours or hamstring-specific counts' -> 51 for no hamstring-specific data and 30 for no exposure hours (Figure 1: 'No hamstring specific data (n = 51)', 'No Exposure hours (n = 30)')",
     "evidenceSummary: reason for descriptive synthesis was 'definitions and exposure recording differed' -> season definition, start and duration ('heterogeneity in the definition of soccer season, the start of the study in the calendar year and duration of data collection')",
     "paper.findings: added the GRADE exceptions ('one subgroup rated low and one subgroup rated moderate', Table 3)",
     "paper.practicalImplications: 'classify injuries ... by time loss' -> state whether time-loss or tissue definition is used; the authors do not prefer time loss ('without registration of tissue injury definition, the burden of injury can be underestimated')",
     "paper.limitations: moved the year-source note to residualConcerns"
   ],
   "residualConcerns":"No publication year is printed: the PDF is the accepted manuscript with line numbers, the copyright line is an unfilled '${year}' template, and the only date is a download stamp of December 15, 2020. Year 2021 is taken from crossrefYear; the article may have been online in 2020. Volume, issue and pages are not printed and were omitted.",
   "spotCheckPriority":"high"
 }
}

 "sourceFile":"Intermittent Fasting and Its    Effects on Athletic Performance- A Review.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"The PDF title 'Intermittent Fasting and Its Effects on Athletic Performance: A Review' (Levy and Chu) matches the filename and the Crossref title.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain":"Nutrition & Hydration",
 "domains":["Nutrition & Hydration","Training & Performance"],
 "audiences":["Nutrition","Sports Medicine","Performance","Athletic Training"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Narrative review of studies of intermittent fasting, including Ramadan fasting, time-restricted eating and alternate-day fasting, across high-intensity, endurance and resistance exercise. Most cited studies are small crossover or observational studies in footballers, cyclists, rowers or resistance-trained men, plus one mouse study. The authors report mixed results, with some studies showing reduced sprint, cycling, rowing or endurance performance and others showing no effect, and no human study showing a performance benefit; only the mouse study found improved endurance.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The review describes no search strategy or inclusion criteria, and its evidence is mostly small studies and Ramadan fasting, which also changes sleep and fluid intake. The authors also define the 5:2 diet inconsistently between the Introduction (alternating days) and the Discussion (5 days fasting, 2 days eating).",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read 'no benefit' as proof that intermittent fasting harms performance, when the authors describe mixed results from mostly small, short-term studies.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2019,
   "citation":"Levy E, Chu T. Intermittent Fasting and Its Effects on Athletic Performance: A Review. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2019;18(7):266-269.",
   "doi":"10.1249/jsr.0000000000000614",
   "abstract":"The authors review studies on intermittent fasting and athletic performance across high-intensity, endurance and resistance exercise. Most data come from Ramadan fasting and overnight fasts. They report varied outcomes, with no study showing an improvement in performance, and call for long-term studies of specific fasting protocols.",
   "tldr":"Intermittent fasting does not appear to improve athletic performance and impaired sprint, cycling, rowing or endurance output in some studies. There are no data on intermittent fasting as a rapid weight-loss method before weigh-ins.",
   "methods":"Narrative review of published studies, grouped by exercise type (high-intensity, endurance and resistance) and by fasting type (Ramadan, time-restricted and alternate-day). The authors cite a 2018 systematic review of fasted-state exercise, but no search method or selection criteria are described for this review.",
   "findings":"In Ramadan studies, an earlier review found mostly small, non-significant decreases in sprint performance, while a later crossover study found significantly slower intermittent sprint times during fasting, and one study of Algerian footballers reported a 16% decrease in endurance capacity. In a 2019 crossover study of ten rowers, omitting breakfast impaired evening 2000 m time-trial performance, and cyclists who skipped breakfast had lower evening performance. Resistance training studies over 8 weeks found little or no harm to lean mass or strength, although one reported lower testosterone and IGF-1 at 8 weeks.",
   "limitations":"The authors note varied definitions of fasting, varied outcome measures, few studies of the specific 5:2 and 16:8 regimens, and mostly short-term data. Ramadan studies confound fasting with sleep disruption and dehydration, and the mouse work may not transfer to humans.",
   "practicalImplications":"Clinicians counselling athletes who want to try intermittent fasting should expect neutral or negative effects on performance rather than a benefit, especially for sprint and endurance work. The review found no data on using intermittent fasting for rapid weight loss in weight-class sports.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: if an athlete fasts, watch high-intensity and endurance output across fasting and fed days, since several studies found impairments and none found a benefit in humans. Resistance training appeared less affected, though the studies were short.",
   "rtp":"Return to Sport Application: the review does not address injury or return to sport and cannot inform return-to-play decisions."
 },
 "verification":{
   "status":"CORRECTED",
   "changes":[
     "evidenceSummary: 'no study showing a performance benefit' conflicted with the mouse study it lists -> 'no human study' ('mice with ADF deprivation ran significantly further')",
     "paper.tldr and paper.practicalImplications: 'current data do not support its use for rapid weight loss' -> no data ('there is a paucity of data regarding using IFast to rapidly drop weight ... it is unclear if it could be used')",
     "paper.findings: added the significant Aziz et al. sprint result ('Sprint times ... were significantly slower in the fasting period')",
     "paper.limitations: removed 'small samples' as an author-stated limitation (not stated) -> varied definitions, outcome measures, few 5:2 and 16:8 studies, short-term data",
     "paper.practicalImplications: tracking advice not in the paper -> the authors' point that clinicians should be aware of 'the negative or neutral effects on athletic performance'"
   ],
   "residualConcerns":"",
   "spotCheckPriority":"normal"
 }
}

content.text:
All eight records are written to `verified/`. One decision changed (Q20); the other seven stay INCLUDE with corrections.

- **Q17**: INCLUDE, CORRECTED, high. "Most validation work is industry sponsored" overstated the paper, which says "many" studies are; fixed. Set high because the record mentions concussion detection, which the paper says wearables are "likely not sensitive or specific" for.
- **Q18**: INCLUDE, CORRECTED, normal. The Horizon A error figures were jumbled; per Table 2 bone mineral content error rose 4.35%, fat mass 0.31% and lean mass under 0.01%. Also noted that every participant was shorter than 193 cm, so the method was never tested on people who actually don't fit on the table. Fixed the athleteDev line too: the combined scan only works on the older Lunar Prodigy.
- **Q19**: INCLUDE, CORRECTED, high. Population tag changed from Professional / Elite to Mixed / Unspecified, because the sample is staff, not athletes. The PDF says 2024 and Crossref says 2025; I kept 2024 and flagged it.
- **Q20**: DEGRADED (was INCLUDE), DECISION_CHANGED, high. The external DOI is wrong. Crossref registers 10.1016/j.jbmt.2018.09.037 to the Journal of Bodywork and Movement Therapies 22(4):858, a one-page item with the same title and authors. The PDF is the 7-page article in the Journal of Sports Science and Medicine (2018;17:298-304). I cleared the DOI and set `doiMissing` to true; Crossref has no DOI for the JSSM article. I also fixed the claims: the significant result was the larger gain in the collagen group. At 6 months its mean instability score (20.76) was still below placebo (21.45) and still in the instability range. Removed advice about bracing that the paper doesn't give.
- **Q21**: INCLUDE, CORRECTED, high. The exclusion count was wrong: the PRISMA flow chart shows 51 studies excluded for no hamstring-specific data and 30 for no exposure hours, not 51 combined. Also corrected the stated reason for the descriptive synthesis. No year is printed in the PDF (it's the accepted manuscript), so 2021 comes from Crossref and is flagged.
- **Q22**: INCLUDE, CORRECTED, high. The draft said hamstring surgery was for "failed or high-demand cases"; the statement actually limits it to specific proximal tendon tears and avulsions. Rewrote the return-to-sport field around what the statement actually says. Set high because it includes same-day return criteria for recurrent shoulder dislocation and medication guidance.
- **Q23**: INCLUDE, CORRECTED, normal. "No study showed a benefit" now reads "no human study" (the mouse study did show one). "Data do not support fasting for rapid weight loss" now reads "no data", which is what the paper says. Added the sprint study that found significantly slower times during fasting.
- **Q24**: INCLUDE, CORRECTED, high. Removed "use under clinical oversight", which the paper doesn't say, and fixed the training-to-failure claim. The PDF is a page proof with no year printed, so 2008 comes from Crossref and is flagged.

All files are valid JSON with no em dashes. My working text copies are in `helpers/v03/`.
